analysis.one_liner: Tightens airline pilot training and rest rules and forces ticket sellers to disclose who operates each flight.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 409-11 on October 14, 2009, but the Senate never voted, and it died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require passenger airlines to give pilots stronger training in handling stalls and upsets, set a minimum of 1,500 flight hours before a pilot can fly for an airline, put limits on how long pilots can be on duty to prevent fatigue, and build a national database of pilot records that airlines must check before hiring. It would also force ticket sellers to tell passengers which airline actually operates each leg of a trip before they buy, and require mentoring programs for newly hired pilots. The House approved it almost unanimously; the Senate took no action.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers, who would fly with better-trained, better-rested pilots and know exactly which airline is operating each segment before buying a ticket; and pilots, who would get stronger training, fatigue limits, mentoring from senior pilots, and a records system with rights to review and correct their own files.

how_it_helps.text: Requires air carriers to train flight crews to recognize and recover from aircraft stalls and upsets and to run remedial training for pilots with performance deficiencies.
Sets a minimum of 1,500 flight hours for an airline transport pilot certificate, with credit the FAA may grant for specific academic training courses.
Requires new regulations limiting pilot flight and duty hours to address fatigue, plus airline fatigue risk management plans with civil penalties for violations.
Makes it an unfair trade practice to sell a ticket without first disclosing the name of the air carrier operating each flight segment, including on websites.
Establishes an electronic pilot records database that air carriers must check before hiring, with pilot consent requirements and the right to review and correct inaccuracies.
Requires mentoring programs pairing experienced pilots with newly hired pilots, and safety management systems at all commercial carriers.

analysis.who_pays: The airlines, especially smaller regional carriers, would bear the compliance costs of new training, fatigue limits, mentoring programs, and record reporting, which could translate into higher fares or thinner margins. People training to become airline pilots would need to accumulate more flight hours before qualifying, raising the time and cost of entering the career, though the bill lets the FAA credit some academic training toward the hours requirement.

drawbacks.text: The bill's costs fall on carriers, and the 1,500-hour rule extends and raises the price of the training path into an airline pilot career; the bill itself directs a study of student financial aid and loan options for flight school students.

The FAA may credit specific academic training courses toward the 1,500-hour requirement, a carve-out that could dilute the hours rule for university-trained pilots; the bill directs an expert panel to assess it.
Much of the bill works through task forces, studies, and rulemaking proceedings with deadlines stretching up to 36 months, rather than requirements that take effect immediately.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is strong: the bill implements board recommendations on crew training, adds fatigue limits, and closes the gap where passengers did not know which airline was actually flying their plane. The main real costs are compliance expenses for carriers and a longer, more expensive training path for aspiring pilots, partly offset by the academic-credit provision. On balance the benefits to passengers and working pilots clearly outweigh the costs, though a fair critic would note how much of the bill is studies and rulemakings rather than immediate rules.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it nearly unanimously, but after the Senate received it in October 2009 it was referred to the Commerce Committee and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee reported the bill on October 6, 2009.

On October 14, 2009, the House passed the bill under a procedure requiring a two-thirds majority, voting 409-11, with 246 House Democrats voting yes and none voting no, and 163 House Republicans voting yes against 11 no.

The Senate received the bill on October 15, 2009, read it twice, and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress.

The bill's provisions follow safety recommendations made by the National Transportation Safety Board, and the bill requires the Secretary of Transportation to report annually to Congress and the board on which safety recommendations have been adopted or refused.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The airline industry gained a delay, since no rules in this bill took effect; much of the same safety package was enacted through a separate 2010 law, so passengers ultimately waited roughly a year longer for protections the House had backed almost unanimously, while regional carriers bought time.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines gained delay; rules came later anyway

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was overwhelmingly bipartisan: 246 House Democrats and 163 House Republicans voted yes, with 0 Democratic no votes and 11 Republican no votes.

industries.note: Regional carriers operating short commuter flights under major-carrier brands would face the heaviest compliance costs in training, mentoring, fatigue limits, and the 1,500-hour hiring floor. They also benefited from passengers not knowing which carrier actually operated a code-shared flight, which the disclosure requirement would end.

All large passenger carriers would fund stall and upset training, remedial and command training, safety management systems, fatigue risk management plans with civil penalties, and pilot record reporting. The costs serve passenger safety, so their interest in avoiding them runs against the public's.

industries.industry: Collegiate flight schools and university aviation programs
industries.note: The bill lets the FAA credit specific academic training courses toward the 1,500-flight-hour requirement, making accredited university flight programs a faster and cheaper route to an airline career. This creates demand for their programs while slightly diluting the hours rule's plain effect.

industries.industry: Ticket sellers, including online travel sites
industries.note: Ticket agents and websites would have to display the operating carrier for every flight segment before purchase, a minor compliance cost that directly serves the buying public.

Pilots gain fatigue limits, professional mentoring programs, higher qualification floors that strengthen the market for experienced pilots, and seats on the bill's task forces and professional development committees. Their interest lines up with passengers' on safety.
